13.2.1. Read Committed Isolation Level #

Read Committed is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL. When a transaction uses this isolation level, a SELECT query (without a FOR UPDATE/SHARE clause) sees only data committed before the query began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the query's execution. In effect, a SELECT query sees a snapshot of the database as of the instant the query begins to run. However, SELECT does see the effects of previous updates executed within its own transaction, even though they are not yet committed. Also note that two successive SELECT commands can see different data, even though they are within a single transaction, if other transactions commit changes after the first SELECT starts and before the second SELECT starts.

Because Read Committed mode starts each command with a new snapshot that includes all transactions committed up to that instant, subsequent commands in the same transaction will see the effects of the committed concurrent transaction in any case. The point at issue above is whether or not a single command sees an absolutely consistent view of the database.

The partial transaction isolation provided by Read Committed mode is adequate for many applications, and this mode is fast and simple to use; however, it is not sufficient for all cases. Applications that do complex queries and updates might require a more rigorously consistent view of the database than Read Committed mode provides.

13.2.2. Repeatable Read Isolation Level #

The Repeatable Read isolation level only sees data committed before the transaction began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the transaction's execution. (However, each query does see the effects of previous updates executed within its own transaction, even though they are not yet committed.) This is a stronger guarantee than is required by the SQL standard for this isolation level, and prevents all of the phenomena described in Table 13.1 except for serialization anomalies. As mentioned above, this is specifically allowed by the standard, which only describes the minimum protections each isolation level must provide.

This level is different from Read Committed in that a query in a repeatable read transaction sees a snapshot as of the start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction, not as of the start of the current statement within the transaction. Thus, successive SELECT commands within a single transaction see the same data, i.e., they do not see changes made by other transactions that committed after their own transaction started.

Applications using this level must be prepared to retry transactions due to serialization failures.

UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, SELECT FOR UPDATE, and SELECT FOR SHARE commands behave the same as SELECT in terms of searching for target rows: they will only find target rows that were committed as of the transaction start time. However, such a target row might have already been updated (or deleted or locked) by another concurrent transaction by the time it is found. In this case, the repeatable read transaction will wait for the first updating transaction to commit or roll back (if it is still in progress). If the first updater rolls back, then its effects are negated and the repeatable read transaction can proceed with updating the originally found row. But if the first updater commits (and actually updated or deleted the row, not just locked it) then the repeatable read transaction will be rolled back with the message

because a repeatable read transaction cannot modify or lock rows changed by other transactions after the repeatable read transaction began.

When an application receives this error message, it should abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning. The second time through, the transaction will see the previously-committed change as part of its initial view of the database, so there is no logical conflict in using the new version of the row as the starting point for the new transaction's update.

Note that only updating transactions might need to be retried; read-only transactions will never have serialization conflicts.

The Repeatable Read mode provides a rigorous guarantee that each transaction sees a completely stable view of the database. However, this view will not necessarily always be consistent with some serial (one at a time) execution of concurrent transactions of the same level. For example, even a read-only transaction at this level may see a control record updated to show that a batch has been completed but not see one of the detail records which is logically part of the batch because it read an earlier revision of the control record. Attempts to enforce business rules by transactions running at this isolation level are not likely to work correctly without careful use of explicit locks to block conflicting transactions.

questions.answer: First SELECT returns 50. Second SELECT returns 999. The two values may differ because, at Read Committed, each SELECT begins with a new snapshot: the first SELECT starts before B's UPDATE has committed, so it sees only the pre-update committed value; by the time the second SELECT starts, B has already committed the new balance, so that new snapshot includes 999.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is that Read Committed takes a new snapshot at the start of each command. A's first SELECT runs before B commits, so A cannot see 999; it sees the last committed value 50. After B commits, A's second SELECT takes a fresh snapshot and is allowed to include B's committed change, so it returns 999. The differing values are therefore expected, not a violation, because the two SELECTs are separate commands with separate snapshots. [context_80f09f9abd69f4e4cd054fd404a1f718]

expected_steps: Identify that the first SELECT starts before B commits and therefore sees the initially committed value (50).
Identify that B commits after the first SELECT and before the second SELECT completes, so A's second SELECT takes a new snapshot that includes 999.
State the allowed non-repeatable-read outcome for two successive SELECTs in one Read Committed transaction.

response.title: PostgreSQL Read Committed: Two-Session Snapshot Observation

questions.stem:
Sessions S1 and S2 run concurrently on a PostgreSQL database under Read Committed isolation. All statements below are ordinary SELECT statements without FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE. Assume each individual SELECT lasts only an instant and no statement is aborted.

1. At time t1, S2 commits an INSERT that adds row R to table T.
2. At time t2 (t2 > t1), S1 begins a transaction and issues SELECT * FROM T; this statement starts at time t3 (t3 > t2).
3. At time t4 (t4 > t3), S2 commits an UPDATE to row R.
4. At time t5 (t5 > t4), S1 issues the same SELECT * FROM T again; this statement starts at time t6 (t6 > t5).

Question: For the first SELECT at t3 and for the second SELECT at t6, state whether each can observe row R in its updated form. Explain what determines visibility at each SELECT, and state whether the two SELECTs may return different versions of row R within the same S1 transaction under Read Committed.
questions.answer: First SELECT at t3: R is visible in the form committed at t1, because Read Committed starts each command with a snapshot that includes all transactions committed before that command began, and t1 < t3. Second SELECT at t6: R is visible in the form committed at t4, because a new snapshot for that command includes S2's t4 commit, and t4 < t6. The two SELECTs can return different versions of R in the same S1 transaction; Read Committed uses a new snapshot per command, so a later command can see a change committed by another transaction after the earlier command started.
questions.explanation: Under Read Committed, each command starts with its own snapshot of committed data, so the first SELECT sees R as committed at t1, while the second SELECT sees R as updated by S2 at t4. Because successive SELECTs in one transaction each get a fresh snapshot, they may return different versions of R even though S1 has not ended. S1's own uncommitted changes would also be visible but are not used here.

Identify that the second SELECT at t6 sees R as committed at t4.
Conclude that the two SELECTs may differ because each command in S1 gets a new snapshot.

For the first SELECT at t3: row R can be observed only in its post-INSERT committed form, if it exists in T; the later UPDATE at t4 has not yet occurred, so it cannot be seen. The key determinant is the snapshot taken when the SELECT statement begins: under Read Committed, a SELECT without FOR UPDATE/SHARE sees data committed before the query began and never sees changes committed during the query’s execution.

For the second SELECT at t6: because t6 is after S2 committed the UPDATE at t4, that new snapshot includes the committed UPDATE, so this SELECT can observe row R in its updated form. Again, visibility is determined by the snapshot taken at the start of the individual SELECT.

Within the same S1 transaction under Read Committed, the two SELECTs may return different versions of row R. PostgreSQL Read Committed takes a new snapshot for each command, so successive SELECTs in one transaction can see different committed data if another transaction commits between the starts of those SELECTs. The supplied material explicitly notes that two successive SELECT commands can see different data within a single transaction under Read Committed.

Sessions S1 and S2 run concurrently on a PostgreSQL database under Read Committed isolation. All statements below are ordinary SELECT statements without FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE. Assume each individual SELECT lasts only an instant and no statement is aborted.

1. At time t1, S2 commits an INSERT that adds row R to table T.
2. At time t2 (t2 > t1), S1 begins a transaction and issues SELECT * FROM T; this statement starts at time t3 (t3 > t2).
3. At time t4 (t4 > t3), S2 commits an UPDATE to row R.
4. At time t5 (t5 > t4), S1 issues the same SELECT * FROM T again; this statement starts at time t6 (t6 > t5).

Question: For the first SELECT at t3 and for the second SELECT at t6, state whether each can observe row R in its updated form. Explain what determines visibility at each SELECT, and state whether the two SELECTs may return different versions of row R within the same S1 transaction under Read Committed.

Second SELECT at t6: R is visible in the form committed at t4, because a new snapshot for that command includes S2's t4 commit, and t4 < t6. The two SELECTs can return different versions of R in the same S1 transaction; Read Committed uses a new snapshot per command, so a later command can see a change committed by another transaction after the earlier command started.

13.2.1. Read Committed Isolation Level #

Read Committed is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL. When a transaction uses this isolation level, a SELECT query (without a FOR UPDATE/SHARE clause) sees only data committed before the query began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the query's execution. In effect, a SELECT query sees a snapshot of the database as of the instant the query begins to run. However, SELECT does see the effects of previous updates executed within its own transaction, even though they are not yet committed. Also note that two successive SELECT commands can see different data, even though they are within a single transaction, if other transactions commit changes after the first SELECT starts and before the second SELECT starts.

Because Read Committed mode starts each command with a new snapshot that includes all transactions committed up to that instant, subsequent commands in the same transaction will see the effects of the committed concurrent transaction in any case. The point at issue above is whether or not a single command sees an absolutely consistent view of the database.

The partial transaction isolation provided by Read Committed mode is adequate for many applications, and this mode is fast and simple to use; however, it is not sufficient for all cases. Applications that do complex queries and updates might require a more rigorously consistent view of the database than Read Committed mode provides.

13.2.2. Repeatable Read Isolation Level #

The Repeatable Read isolation level only sees data committed before the transaction began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the transaction's execution. (However, each query does see the effects of previous updates executed within its own transaction, even though they are not yet committed.) This is a stronger guarantee than is required by the SQL standard for this isolation level, and prevents all of the phenomena described in Table 13.1 except for serialization anomalies. As mentioned above, this is specifically allowed by the standard, which only describes the minimum protections each isolation level must provide.

This level is different from Read Committed in that a query in a repeatable read transaction sees a snapshot as of the start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction, not as of the start of the current statement within the transaction. Thus, successive SELECT commands within a single transaction see the same data, i.e., they do not see changes made by other transactions that committed after their own transaction started.

Applications using this level must be prepared to retry transactions due to serialization failures.

UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, SELECT FOR UPDATE, and SELECT FOR SHARE commands behave the same as SELECT in terms of searching for target rows: they will only find target rows that were committed as of the transaction start time. However, such a target row might have already been updated (or deleted or locked) by another concurrent transaction by the time it is found. In this case, the repeatable read transaction will wait for the first updating transaction to commit or roll back (if it is still in progress). If the first updater rolls back, then its effects are negated and the repeatable read transaction can proceed with updating the originally found row. But if the first updater commits (and actually updated or deleted the row, not just locked it) then the repeatable read transaction will be rolled back with the message

because a repeatable read transaction cannot modify or lock rows changed by other transactions after the repeatable read transaction began.

When an application receives this error message, it should abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning. The second time through, the transaction will see the previously-committed change as part of its initial view of the database, so there is no logical conflict in using the new version of the row as the starting point for the new transaction's update.

Note that only updating transactions might need to be retried; read-only transactions will never have serialization conflicts.

The Repeatable Read mode provides a rigorous guarantee that each transaction sees a completely stable view of the database. However, this view will not necessarily always be consistent with some serial (one at a time) execution of concurrent transactions of the same level. For example, even a read-only transaction at this level may see a control record updated to show that a batch has been completed but not see one of the detail records which is logically part of the batch because it read an earlier revision of the control record. Attempts to enforce business rules by transactions running at this isolation level are not likely to work correctly without careful use of explicit locks to block conflicting transactions.
